planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is reliably warm; Aunt Hettie's Red is a Tennessee heirloom preserved for decades in one family's garden before wider seed-saver distribution, and it stays more compact than many other red-podded okra strains.

directions: Soak seeds overnight before direct sowing 1 inch deep after the last frost, thinning plants to 12-18 inches apart. Aunt Hettie's Red traces back to a Tennessee home garden, where it was kept true for generations before seed-saving groups began sharing it more widely, and it is now grown as far south as the Gulf Coast. Compared with taller red heirlooms, its plants stay a manageable 4-5 feet with deep red stems and leaf veins, setting plump, meaty burgundy pods that should be cut before they exceed 4 inches to keep them tender. In blind tasting panels among dozens of okra varieties it has repeatedly placed among the most flavorful reds, making it worth growing for the table as much as for its ornamental color.

common_name: White Triumph Sweet Potato (Vintage Dry-Type Southern Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F, in loose, well-drained soil formed into ridges in full sun; White Triumph is one of the older dry-fleshed sweet potato types still kept in circulation by heirloom growers.

directions: Set slips 12-18 inches apart in loose, sandy-loam soil hilled into ridges, and hold off on nitrogen-rich fertilizer since it pushes vine growth at the expense of root formation. White Triumph is a vintage dry-type sweet potato with tan to yellowish-white skin and snow-white flesh that cooks up firm and mealy rather than moist, closer in texture to a baking potato than to a modern orange-fleshed variety, with a mild, only lightly sweet flavor. Vines are vigorous and the roots are known to resist soil rot and scurf better than many old white-fleshed types, giving reliable mid-season yields around 90-105 days. Dig before the first frost once vines start to yellow, then cure in a warm, humid spot for a week or two to firm the skin and improve keeping quality.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Sweet Potato Production

common_name: Red Wine Velvet Sweet Potato (Deep Red-Skin Orange-Flesh Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F, in loose, well-drained soil formed into ridges in full sun; Red Wine Velvet is a mid-season vining heirloom kept alive mainly by small seed-saving growers.

directions: Plant slips 12-18 inches apart in loose, well-drained soil ridged up for good drainage, and avoid heavily nitrogen-rich amendments that favor foliage over root bulking. Red Wine Velvet is a mid-season, normal-leaf vining heirloom sweet potato prized for its deep wine-red skin wrapped around moist, richly colored orange flesh, offering a striking contrast to the paler skin of standard commercial types like Beauregard. Yields run average rather than exceptional, which is part of why the variety has stayed a small-grower specialty rather than a commercial staple, but the flavor is sweet and the deep-red roots make an eye-catching addition to a home harvest basket. Dig once vines begin to yellow in fall and cure in warm, humid conditions for one to two weeks before storing to sweeten the flesh and toughen the skin.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Sweet Potato Production

common_name: All Purple Sweet Potato (Whole-Root Purple-Skin Purple-Flesh Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F, in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; All Purple is a distinct named purple sweet potato sold alongside (but separate from) Stokes Purple and Okinawan types.

directions: Set slips 12-18 inches apart in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping fertility moderate since overly rich soil favors vine growth over root formation. All Purple is a heirloom sweet potato selection distributed by small specialty growers as its own distinct cultivar alongside other named purple types like Molokai Purple and Purple Passion, producing roots with purple skin over dense, uniformly deep-purple flesh from center to edge. The texture is drier and firmer than orange-fleshed sweet potatoes, with an earthy, mildly sweet flavor that holds its color well when roasted or steamed, though it fades somewhat when boiled in acidic water. Sprawling vines with purple-tinged, deeply lobed leaves make it a dual-purpose plant, since the young leaves and shoot tips are also edible and commonly cooked as greens. Harvest after vines begin to yellow and before frost, then cure in warm, humid conditions for a week or two to develop full sweetness and improve storage life.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Sweet Potato Production
